inbox.content: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.

history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a Harvard University scientific proposal to study how tiny amounts of aerosol particles behave in the stratosphere. Principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators including David Keith described the concept publicly, including at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. A very small amount of material — on the order of 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms, typically calcium carbonate (a common mineral found in limestone and used in products such as toothpaste) — would be released into a small mixed volume roughly 1 km long and 100 meters in diameter. The gondola would then fly back through that plume to measure aerosol microphysics, chemistry, and light scattering. A 2021 platform test in Sweden, planned with the Swedish Space Corporation from Esrange, was a hardware test only: the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended suspending it pending societal engagement, and no particles were to be released. In March 2024 Harvard announced that Keutsch was no longer pursuing SCoPEx; the platform is expected to be repurposed for stratospheric research unrelated to solar geoengineering.

history.contentIn: The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change adopted by 196 Parties at COP21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and in force from 4 November 2016. Its central aim is to hold the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C. Parties submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) describing their mitigation plans; the Agreement uses a ratchet mechanism of successive NDCs rather than a single top-down allocation of tonnes. The treaty does not ban talking about geoengineering, but it is not a secret authorisation to spray the atmosphere. Article 4 addresses peaking of greenhouse gas emissions and a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks in the second half of the century (often discussed as net-zero CO2). The United States joined, withdrew under the first Trump administration, and rejoined under the Biden administration; participation has been politically contested but the scientific case for rapid emissions cuts is independent of any one administration. Meeting Paris temperature goals requires deep, sustained cuts in fossil CO2, methane and other greenhouse gases, plus protection of carbon sinks — not covert aviation spraying.
